sections.heading: Resting in what you have given me
sections.text:
Almighty God, Father, today I can hardly ask for anything before I first thank you. You have loved me with a love that did not begin with me and will not end with me. You have covered me in the righteousness of Jesus. You have given me peace with you, comfort that is more than I deserve, and a joy I cannot fully explain.

When I see clearly that I am saved and accepted by you, my prayers turn into praise. Christ’s kindness toward me feels like light from heaven falling on my soul, and I can only say: thank you.
theological_themes: Assurance of salvation rests in God's everlasting love, Christ's righteousness, and the peace of justification.
Praise rises naturally when the believer has a clear sense of being reconciled to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul connects justification by faith with peace with God and access into grace. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that acceptance with God is not based on the believer’s mood or performance, but on what God has done in Christ.
God’s covenant love for his people is described as everlasting, which supports the prayer’s language of being loved with a love that precedes and outlasts the believer’s own faithfulness.
This passage teaches that Christ took the place of sinners so that they might become righteous in him. It supports the prayer’s claim that the believer is clothed in a righteousness not their own.

sections.heading: Thanking you for choosing and keeping me
sections.text:
Father, your choosing grace is not cold or abstract when I receive it from your Word and see its fruit in my own heart. It is sweet because it tells me that my salvation began in your mercy, not in my strength.

Thank you that you keep the sinner you have loved. Thank you that you have taken responsibility for bringing me home. If my final arrival depended on my grip on you, I would never make it. But you hold me, and you will not let me go.
theological_themes: Election is received as comfort when rooted in Scripture and experienced as God's gracious initiative.
Perseverance depends on God's preserving grace, not the believer's unaided strength.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God for choosing his people in Christ before the foundation of the world and adopting them according to his will. This supports the prayer’s wonder that salvation begins in God’s gracious purpose.
Jesus promises that his sheep are held securely in his hand and the Father’s hand. This directly grounds the prayer’s confidence that God keeps those he has loved.
Paul expresses confidence that God will complete the good work he began. This supports the prayer’s dependence on God to bring salvation to its intended end.

sections.heading: Telling the truth about myself and about Christ
sections.text:
Lord, help me not to deny what your grace has really done in me. You have given me new life, and it would be wrong to act as if nothing has changed.

But I also know this: if Jesus were not my righteousness and my redemption, I would be lost under the weight of my sins—my wrong actions, my failures, my unbelief, and my coldness toward you and others. And if Jesus, by the power of the Holy Spirit, were not making me holy, there is no sin I could safely say I would never commit.

So I do not boast in myself. I boast in Christ. He is my only safety, my only standing before you, and my only hope for becoming clean.
theological_themes: The believer acknowledges both real regeneration and total dependence on Christ.
Christ is the believer's righteousness, redemption, and sanctification.
Honest self-knowledge includes recognizing the depth of remaining sin and the need for the Spirit's power.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says Christ has become wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for believers, so boasting belongs only in the Lord. This closely matches the prayer’s dependence on Christ for every part of salvation.
This passage links salvation to God’s mercy, regeneration by the Spirit, justification by grace, and the hope of eternal life. It supports the prayer’s refusal to treat new life as self-produced.

Paul describes the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit and calls believers to walk by the Spirit. This illuminates the prayer’s confession that apart from the Spirit’s sanctifying work, sin would dominate.

sections.heading: Longing to become like Jesus
sections.text:
Father, when will I think more like Jesus? When will my loves, my reactions, my desires, and my whole life look more like him?

Please keep changing me. Do not let me be satisfied with merely knowing that I am forgiven while I remain careless about holiness. Make me more like your Son, not only in what I believe, but in what I want and how I live.
theological_themes: Assurance does not produce complacency but a deeper longing for likeness to Christ.
Sanctification is God’s ongoing work of conforming believers to the image of his Son.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God’s purpose for his people is conformity to the image of his Son. This grounds the prayer’s longing to become like Jesus as part of God’s saving purpose.
Believers are transformed into Christ’s image by the Lord who is the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s request for ongoing inward change rather than mere outward improvement.

sections.heading: Counting Christ better than everything else
sections.text:
Lord Jesus, all the good things this life can offer are small compared with your love. One glimpse of your grace is worth more than anything I could possess.

If I had the wealth of countless worlds, I would not be richer than I already am in you. Your riches are mine by grace. A single moment of real fellowship with you, a single clear sight of your kindness toward me, is beyond price.
theological_themes: Christ’s love and grace surpass all earthly possessions and comforts.
The believer’s true wealth, happiness, and contentment are found in communion with Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts all things as loss compared with gaining Christ and being found in him. This supports the prayer’s claim that Christ is worth more than every earthly good.
Paul speaks of the unsearchable riches of Christ, which fits the prayer’s language of possessing immeasurable wealth in him by grace.
The psalmist confesses that God himself is his supreme desire and portion. This supports the prayer’s contentment in God above every created treasure.

sections.heading: Recognizing that even my desire for you is grace
sections.text:
But Father, I know I would not even want your presence if you had not first let me taste its sweetness. I could not know that sweetness unless your Spirit had made it real in my heart. I would not love you at all unless you had first loved me, chosen me, called me, adopted me, and saved me.

So I bless you for the covenant of grace. You have not dealt with me according to what I deserved. You have bound yourself to sinners through Christ, and you have brought me in. Keep me near you, and let my whole life answer your grace with grateful love. Amen.
theological_themes: Desire for God is itself the fruit of God's prior grace and the Spirit's work in the heart.
Calling, adoption, and salvation flow from God's gracious initiative.
The covenant of grace is praised as God's merciful commitment to save sinners through Christ.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that believers love because God first loved them. This directly supports the prayer’s confession that love for God is a response to prior grace.
Paul describes believers receiving the Spirit of adoption and becoming heirs with Christ. This grounds the prayer’s gratitude for being adopted and brought into God’s family.

Paul links predestination, calling, justification, and glorification as God’s saving work from beginning to end. This supports the prayer’s sequence of being chosen, called, and saved by God’s initiative.

Hebrews describes the new covenant in which God writes his law on his people’s hearts, claims them as his own, and forgives their sins. This illuminates the prayer’s final praise for the covenant of grace.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes election and God’s preserving grace. These are historically Reformed emphases and can be doctrinally contested among Christians, so the adaptation preserves them without trying to soften or broaden them beyond the original’s intent.

The phrase 'covenant of grace' is a theological term especially associated with Reformed covenant theology. It was retained because it is central to the original’s conclusion, while the prayer text briefly explains it in relational and biblical terms.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original’s line about 'wronging the work of grace' was rendered as refusing to deny that God has truly given new life. This preserves the balance between humility about sin and honest acknowledgment of regeneration.

The original’s severe statement that apart from Christ the speaker would 'sink into nethermost hell' was expressed as being lost under the weight of sin. This keeps the theological force of deserved judgment while using language a contemporary believer could naturally pray.

The original’s claim that apart from the Spirit there is no sin the speaker would not commit was kept substantially intact, because it expresses a Puritan view of remaining sin and dependence on sanctifying grace rather than a rhetorical exaggeration to be removed.
